newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban unsure of future political system - minister.
newsitem.headline: Taleban unsure of future political system - minister.

text.p: A senior Taleban official said on Thursday that all Afghans would have the right to choose the future path of their country, but his administration had yet to decide how the public would be represented.

"When peace and security has been established, there will be no problems for everyone to return. When they come back, they will have full rights to take part and give their views on a future government," acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Abbas Stanakzai told Reuters.

"But we have not decided on the mechanism, it is before time. Right now we are struggling to bring peace and security. When that has been established, then we will work on the mechanism," said Stanakzai.
The Taleban, which captured the capital Kabul on September 27, have vowed to impose their strict version of Islam across the country.

They control more than 75 per cent of Afghanistan but are battling an alliance consisting of forces loyal to the government they ousted from Kabul, the northern forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite fighters under Karim Khalili in the centre of the country.
The radical Taleban have yet to be recognised as the legitimate government by any country or international body.

Western nations have criticised the Taleban's treatment of women since they took over Kabul. Apart from a strict dress code, authorities have placed restrictions on women working and closed schools for girls.
Stanakzai reiterated that the head of state was Mullah Mohammed Omar, the leader of the Taleban, while a six-man interim ruling council in Kabul ran the nation's day-to-day affairs.
He said it was too early to tell if there would be elections if and when peace had been established. He said the people would have to decide.

"It would be before time if I said that there will be free elections... When we have peace, and people return to their homes, they will sit together and decide how to select the government and what type of system they should adopt for the country," he said.

However, Stanakzai did say that Mullah Omar, who has been given the title of Amir el Momineen -- leader of the faithful -- by his followers, could only be removed from office by the supreme Islamic court.

"According to Islamic principles, the man who is appointed as Amir el Momineen will be head of state as long as he is acting according to Islamic principles. If anyone objects to his rule, they can challenge him in the high court," Stanakzai said.
All officials, including those of the high court, are appointed by Mullah Omar.
He was nominated as head of state by a council of 1,600 elders and religious leaders who convened in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar -- a Taleban stronghold -- last year.
Stanakzai also said the Taleban were doing their best to control unruly elements in their ranks.
"We have certain problems, especially with those who are working with us in the security forces and on the front line," he said.
"Many of these people are volunteers from the tribal areas and the villages, and they have not been trained."
